chapters.name: Chapter 1: Finding careers that fit you

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Starting with what you like
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Take a free interest quiz and list your top interests.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free interest quiz such as the one on mynextmove.org, you will list your top interest areas and the three activities you enjoy most, answering the quiz honestly and writing down the results.
A good career search starts with you: what you enjoy, what you are good at and what matters to you. Maybe you love fixing things, drawing, organizing events, helping friends with problems, or figuring out how a game works.
My Next Move is a free career site from the U.S. Department of Labor. Its interest profiler asks you about kinds of work you might enjoy and suggests careers that match. Your school counselor may have other interest quizzes too.
Write down your results and the three activities you enjoy most. These are your starting clues.
Step by step:
- Go to mynextmove.org.
- Open the interest profiler and answer honestly.
- Write down your top interest areas.
- Add three activities you enjoy most.
Words to know:
- Interest profiler: a quiz that matches what you like with kinds of work.
- Career: the kind of work you do over a long time, often with growing skills.
Official sources:
- My Next Move (U.S. Department of Labor)
Try it now: Take the interest profiler on mynextmove.org (or one your counselor gives you). Write down your top interest areas and three things you love doing.
You can now describe your interests in a way that helps you search for careers.

check.q: What is the first step in a good career search?
options: Picking the job that pays the most
Looking at what you enjoy, are good at and care about
check.why: A good search starts with you: your interests, strengths and values.

check.q: You finished the interest profiler on mynextmove.org. What do you do next?
options: Close it and forget the results
Retake it until it says what you want
Share your home address with the site
Write down your top interest areas and three activities you love
check.why: Your results and favorite activities are your starting clues.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Brainstorming careers with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to turn your interests into a list of careers to explore.
This lesson builds toward: Given your interests and an AI assistant you are allowed to use, you will generate a list of careers with different training paths and choose two to research, sharing no private details and treating the list as ideas to check.
Now give your clues to an AI assistant you are allowed to use: "I am 15. I like video games, drawing and helping younger kids. Suggest 10 careers that mix these, from ones that need a short training program to ones that need college."
Ask follow-ups: "Which of these work with AI?" "Which ones can I try in high school?" "Explain what a day looks like in career 3."
AI is good for ideas but can be wrong about pay, training and job numbers. Treat its list as ideas to check, not facts.
Step by step:
- Give AI your age range and interests (no private details).
- Ask for 10 careers with different training paths.
- Ask follow-ups about a typical day and high school steps.
- Pick two to research.
Words to know:
- Training path: the schooling or practice you need for a job, like a certificate, apprenticeship or college degree.
- Apprenticeship: a paid job where you learn a skilled trade while working.
Try it now: Give an AI assistant your interests and ask for 10 careers with different training paths. Ask what a day looks like in two of them, then pick your two favorites.
You can now use AI to brainstorm careers that match your interests.

check.q: How should you treat a list of careers from AI?
check.why: AI is good for ideas but can be wrong about pay, training and job numbers.

check.q: You like music and fixing things. Which prompt helps most?
options: "Give me my address and a job."
"I like music and fixing things. Suggest 10 careers with different training paths."
check.why: Giving your interests and asking for different training paths gets useful ideas.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Checking the facts on official career sites
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Look up a career's pay, training and job outlook on an official site.
This lesson builds toward: For each of your two careers, you will look up typical pay, training and job outlook on bls.gov/ooh or mynextmove.org, trusting the official site wherever it disagrees with AI.
The Occupational Outlook Handbook from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (bls.gov/ooh) is a free, official guide to hundreds of jobs. For each one it shows typical pay, the usual education and training, and how many jobs are expected in the future.
My Next Move also shows what people in each job do, the skills they use and the training they need. Pay changes over time and from place to place, so always look up the current numbers rather than trusting a number from AI or a friend.
Compare what AI told you with what the official site says. Where they disagree, trust the official site.
Step by step:
- Open bls.gov/ooh or mynextmove.org.
- Search for your career.
- Write down pay, typical training and job outlook.
- Compare with what AI said and trust the official site.
Words to know:
- Median pay: the middle pay: half of workers earn more, half earn less.
- Job outlook: how many jobs are expected in the future.
Official sources:
- Occupational Outlook Handbook (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics)
- My Next Move (U.S. Department of Labor)
Try it now: Look up your two careers on bls.gov/ooh or mynextmove.org. Write down the typical training, pay and job outlook for each, and note one thing AI got different.
You can now research a career's real facts on an official site.

check.q: What does the Occupational Outlook Handbook at bls.gov/ooh show?
options: Typical pay, training and job outlook for hundreds of jobs
check.why: It is a free, official guide to jobs from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

check.q: A friend says a career pays a lot, and AI gives a different number. What do you do?
options: Look up the current pay on an official site
check.why: Pay changes over time and place, so check the current number on an official site.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: How AI is changing work
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe one way AI is used in a career you like and the human skills that still matter.
This lesson builds toward: For one career you like, you will describe one way AI is used in that work and two human skills that still matter, checked with a real person or a trusted source.
AI is changing many jobs. Nurses use it to help with records, mechanics use it to find problems in cars, designers use it to try ideas fast, and game studios use it to test levels. Some tasks get done by AI; new tasks appear.
Human skills matter even more: talking with people, solving new problems, being creative, being reliable and knowing when the AI is wrong.
Ask AI: "How is AI used today in [career]? What human skills are still most important?" Then check what it says with a real person in that job or a trusted news or industry site.
Words to know:
- Automation: when machines or software do tasks people used to do.
- Soft skills: people skills like communication, teamwork and dependability.
Try it now: Ask AI how AI is used in one of your two careers and which human skills matter most. Write down one AI use and two human skills, and one question you would ask a real person in that job.
You can now explain how AI touches a career and which human skills still matter.

check.q: Which is a human skill that matters more as AI spreads?
options: Talking with people and solving new problems
check.why: Communication, creativity, reliability and knowing when AI is wrong matter even more.

check.q: AI tells you how it is used in nursing. How do you check it?
options: Ask a real nurse or read a trusted industry or news site
check.why: Check what AI says with a real person in the job or a trusted source.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Building a pathway from high school
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a step-by-step plan from now to a first job in a career.
This lesson builds toward: Given your grade and a target career, you will plan a step-by-step pathway from now to a first job, with three steps for this school year, with at least one step checked with your counselor or an official site.
A career pathway is the road from where you are now to the job you want. It might include classes, clubs, volunteering, a summer program, a certificate, an apprenticeship, community college or a university.
Ask AI: "I am in 10th grade and interested in becoming an electrician. Make a step-by-step path from now to my first job, with things I can do this year." Then check training rules on official sites, because licenses and programs differ by state.
Your school counselor can tell you which classes and programs your school offers, like career and technical education (CTE) or dual enrollment.
Step by step:
- Name your grade and target career.
- Ask AI for a step-by-step path with this-year actions.
- Check training and license rules on official sites.
- Ask your counselor what your school offers.
Words to know:
- Career pathway: the steps from school to a job in a field.
- CTE: career and technical education: school classes that teach job skills.
- Dual enrollment: taking college classes while still in high school.
Try it now: Ask AI for a step-by-step path to one of your careers. Pick three things you can do this school year and check one of them with your counselor or an official site.
You can now build a realistic career pathway plan.

options: The road from where you are now to the job you want
check.why: A pathway lists the steps, such as classes, programs and training, from now to a job.

check.q: AI's pathway says you need a certain license. What do you do?
options: Assume it is the same in every state
Check the license rules on an official site for your state
Ask AI to issue the license
check.why: Licenses and programs differ by state, so check official sites.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Getting ready for a first job
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check the basic youth work rules and prepare a simple first-job pitch.
This lesson builds toward: Before a first job, volunteering or job shadowing, you will check the federal and state youth work rules and write a three-sentence pitch about yourself, following the stricter rule and practicing the pitch out loud.
A first job, volunteering or job shadowing helps you test a career. Under federal law, most jobs need you to be at least 14. If you are 14 or 15, your hours are limited, for example no more than 3 hours on a school day and only between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. for most of the year (until 9 p.m. from June 1 to Labor Day). At 16 and 17, federal law does not limit hours, but no one under 18 may do hazardous jobs.
Many states have stricter rules and may need a work permit. When federal and state laws both apply, the stricter one counts. Check your state's labor office and talk with a parent or guardian.
AI can help you write a short pitch about yourself: "I am 15, I am reliable, I help coach my little brother's soccer team, and I want to learn customer service." Practice saying it out loud. Do not put your address or phone number into the AI.
Step by step:
- Check federal and state youth work rules.
- Talk with a parent or guardian about work or volunteering.
- Use AI to draft a 3-sentence pitch about yourself.
- Practice it out loud.
Words to know:
- Work permit: a paper some states require before a teen can work.
- Job shadowing: following a worker for a day to see what the job is like.
- Hazardous job: work that is dangerous and not allowed for anyone under 18.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Labor Fact Sheet #43: Child labor rules for nonagricultural jobs
- U.S. Department of Labor: Child labor and state laws
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page career plan: why the career fits you, its training, pay and outlook from an official site, one way AI is used in it, and three steps for this school year. Add your 3-sentence first-job pitch at the bottom.
You can now explore careers, check the facts, plan your path and pitch yourself for a first job.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Why it fits me No link between the career and the learner's interests. Names interest quiz results or favorite activities that match the career. Also names a strength or value that fits the career. Official facts Pay, training or outlook is missing or taken only from AI. Typical training, pay and job outlook from bls.gov/ooh or mynextmove.org. Also notes one thing AI got different from the official site. AI in the work No AI use or human skill named. One way AI is used in the career and two human skills that still matter. Includes a question to ask a real person in that job, or their answer. This year's steps Fewer than three steps, or steps are vague like "work hard". Three concrete steps: a class, a club or activity, and a person to talk to. At least one step is checked with a counselor or an official site. First-job pitch No pitch, or it includes private details. A three-sentence pitch about the learner, practiced out loud. Also notes the youth work rules that apply to the learner's age and state. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Under federal law, what kind of work may no one under 18 do?
check.why: Federal law bars anyone under 18 from hazardous jobs.

check.q: You want AI to help write your first-job pitch. What do you leave out of the prompt?
options: That you coach a sports team
check.why: Keep private details like your address and phone number out of AI tools.
